rounds.response: Do not email clinical details to his daughter yet—there is no documented patient authorization and the topics include especially sensitive items (anxiety, alcohol-use history) that should not be disclosed without explicit permission. You may confirm she can help with appointments and send scheduling-related messages now, but document his verbal agreement in the chart immediately and limit messages to administrative details. If the daughter should receive meds or clinical summaries, obtain and record a specific patient authorization (signed release, a witnessed and documented verbal consent on the phone, or formal proxy/portal access) that lists exactly which categories are allowed. If/when the patient authorizes, share only the minimum necessary information and include mental-health or substance-use details only if he explicitly names those categories in the authorization. Suggested staff script: “Mr. Alvarez, do you want us to share your medication list and visit summaries with your daughter? If so, please sign this release or we can add her as a portal proxy.”

If a drug has multiple indications that could reveal a sensitive condition, either omit it or describe it generically only as “medication for blood pressure” or “medication for diabetes” after checking with the patient. In the email include a one-sentence note: “Per Mr. Alvarez’s express instructions, we are not disclosing mental-health or substance-use treatment details.” Document in the chart exactly what you sent, the patient’s verbal authorization and limits, the date/time, and save the outgoing message; ask Mr. Alvarez whether he wants to sign a written release or grant portal proxy access if broader sharing is needed (especially if the daughter helps administer meds).

Phone script for staff: "Per Mr. Alvarez’s instructions, we can share updates about his diabetes and blood pressure and the related medications; he has asked that we not share any mental‑health or substance‑use treatment information.
